concept.name: CDN Architecture & Geo-Distributed Edge Caching
concept.tagline: Slash origin server latency using BGP Anycast routing, edge PoPs, cache-control directives, and stale-while-revalidate invalidation.

spark.summary: A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a globally distributed network of Points of Presence (PoPs) that terminates client TCP/TLS connections physically close to users via BGP Anycast routing. By serving cached static assets and API responses from the network edge, CDNs reduce origin server load by 80-95% and drop round-trip times from hundreds of milliseconds to under 15ms.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use BGP Anycast to terminate user TCP/TLS handshakes at the closest edge PoP; combine Cache-Control directives (s-maxage, stale-while-revalidate) with surrogate keys (Cache-Tags) to achieve instant origin offload without serving stale data.

concept.whyItMatters: The speed of light imposes an immutable physical limit on network packets: transcontinental round-trips (e.g. London to California) cost ~140ms per round trip. Requiring 3-way handshakes, TLS negotiation, and data fetches across oceans creates sluggish multi-second page loads. CDNs place cached data and TLS terminators within 10ms of 95% of global internet users.
whenToUse: Static web assets (images, JavaScript, CSS, fonts, videos) with high read reusability.
High-traffic public API endpoints with moderate freshness tolerances (e.g. product catalogs, leaderboards).
Shielding origin data centers against Layer 3/4 and Layer 7 volumetric DDoS attacks.
whenNotToUse: Strictly personalized user-specific transactional data (e.g. shopping cart checkout, bank account balances) with zero cache reuse.
Internal microservice RPCs operating inside the same private cloud VPC.
Applications with strict data residency regulations that prohibit caching payload data across international borders without sovereignty guarantees.
keyPoints: BGP Anycast Routing: Multiple edge PoPs advertise the exact same IP address via Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). Internet routers automatically steer user packets to the topologically closest PoP.
Cache-Control & Surrogate Directives: Differentiates browser caching from shared edge caching using max-age (browser) vs s-maxage (CDN edge), and stale-while-revalidate for background updates.

Surrogate Keys & Tag-Based Invalidation: Tags cached objects with domain identifiers (e.g. 'article-123', 'author-45'); origin servers issue a single purge request by tag to invalidate thousands of related edge objects in milliseconds.
Tiered Caching & Origin Shields: Edge PoPs query regional shield PoPs instead of directly hammering origin servers on cache misses, consolidating origin read requests.
Edge Compute & Dynamic Request Routing: Lightweight V8 isolates or WebAssembly runtimes execute authentication, header rewriting, and A/B test experiments directly at the edge.

examples.title: Fastly Surrogate Key Purging for E-Commerce Catalogs
examples.scenario: An e-commerce platform with 500,000 product pages suffered from stale cache data whenever inventory or pricing changed.
examples.outcome: Implemented Surrogate-Key headers on product API responses; inventory updates issue targeted purge calls that evict edge copies globally within 150 milliseconds.

examples.title: Stale-While-Revalidate for Zero-Latency API Reads
examples.scenario: A high-traffic news website experienced periodic origin database spikes when cache keys expired during breaking news traffic bursts.
examples.outcome: Configured 'Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600'; edge PoPs serve the cached version instantly while asynchronously fetching fresh content in the background.

tradeOffs.factor: Edge Offload vs Cache Invalidation Complexity
tradeOffs.pro: Offloads 90%+ of network traffic and compute from origin databases, providing infinite read scalability.
tradeOffs.con: Cache invalidation is notoriously difficult; edge propagation delays can lead to inconsistent state between users in different geographies.

tradeOffs.factor: BGP Anycast Routing vs Session Stickiness
tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates DNS latency and automatically routes users around congested or failed internet paths.
tradeOffs.con: BGP route flaps during long-lived TCP downloads can re-route packets to a different PoP mid-stream, breaking connections without persistent state synchronization.

tradeOffs.factor: Origin Shielding vs Extra Cache Hop
tradeOffs.pro: Collapses cache misses from 100 global PoPs into a single origin request.
tradeOffs.con: Adds 5-20ms latency to genuine cache misses that must traverse both the edge PoP and origin shield before reaching origin.

failureModes.name: Thundering Herd on Cache Expiration
failureModes.description: A popular cache key expires simultaneously across all edge PoPs, sending tens of thousands of concurrent miss queries to the origin server.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable origin shielding, request coalescing (waiting for the first request to populate cache), and stale-while-revalidate.

failureModes.name: Cache Poisoning via Unkeyed Headers
failureModes.description: An attacker injects malicious headers (e.g. X-Forwarded-Host) into a request; if the CDN caches the response using only the URL path as the cache key, all subsequent users receive the corrupted payload.
failureModes.mitigation: Explicitly declare and sanitize all cache keys; ensure unkeyed headers are stripped or excluded from cache hashing.

failureModes.name: Purge Latency Lag during Breaking Changes
failureModes.description: A bad frontend deployment requires an immediate purge, but the CDN invalidation API queues lag under load, leaving users with broken assets for minutes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use content-addressed asset versioning (e.g. main.[hash].js) so new code requires no cache invalidation.

commonMistakes: Using fixed URLs without file hashes for static assets, forcing reliance on unreliable cache purge APIs.
Omitting stale-while-revalidate, forcing user requests to block synchronously on origin DB latency during cache misses.
Failing to cache 404 responses (negative caching), allowing attackers to DoS origin servers with floods of bogus URLs.

deepDive.markdownContent:
## 1. Physical Latency & The BGP Anycast Architecture

The primary constraint in global networking is propagation delay: fiber optic cables transmit signals at approximately **200,000 km/s** (2/3 the speed of light in a vacuum).

```architecture
{
  "view": "high-level",
  "title": "BGP Anycast Edge PoP Network Architecture",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "client_eu", "label": "London Client", "type": "client" },
    { "id": "client_us", "label": "New York Client", "type": "client" },
    { "id": "pop_eu", "label": "London Edge PoP (IP: 198.51.100.1)", "type": "service" },
    { "id": "pop_us", "label": "New York Edge PoP (IP: 198.51.100.1)", "type": "service" },
    { "id": "shield", "label": "Origin Shield PoP (Ashburn, VA)", "type": "queue" },
    { "id": "origin", "label": "Origin Database & Server Fleet", "type": "database" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "client_eu", "to": "pop_eu", "label": "BGP Anycast Route (3ms RTT)" },
    { "from": "client_us", "to": "pop_us", "label": "BGP Anycast Route (4ms RTT)" },
    { "from": "pop_eu", "to": "shield", "label": "Consolidated Cache Miss" },
    { "from": "pop_us", "to": "shield", "label": "Consolidated Cache Miss" },
    { "from": "shield", "to": "origin", "label": "Single Origin Request" }
  ]
}
```

### How Anycast Works
In standard **Unicast**, each IP address routes to exactly one server. In **Anycast**, multiple edge servers in London, Tokyo, Frankfurt, and New York advertise the identical IP address via BGP. The user's local ISP router automatically sends traffic to the nearest geographic node based on standard AS-path metrics.

---

## 2. HTTP Cache-Control Header Semantics

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=86400
Surrogate-Key: product-catalog category-electronics
ETag: "33a64df551425fcc55e4d42a148795d9f25f89d4"
```

* **`public`**: Allows both shared edge proxies (CDNs) and private user browsers to cache the response.
* **`max-age=300`**: Browsers can cache the response for **5 minutes** before verifying freshness.
* **`s-maxage=3600`**: CDN shared edge caches can retain the object for **1 hour**, ignoring the browser `max-age`.
* **`stale-while-revalidate=86400`**: If the 1-hour window expires, the CDN serves the stale cached copy instantly to the user while asynchronously dispatching a single background request to origin to refresh the cache.

---

## 3. Surrogate Keys & Instant Tag-Based Purging

Instead of maintaining brittle URL lists for cache eviction, high-throughput architectures attach **Surrogate-Keys**:
1. When generating a product page, the application adds: `Surrogate-Key: product-994 category-audio brand-sony`.
2. The CDN indexes the cached item under all three tags.
3. When the product price changes, the backend emits:
```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.fastly.com/service/$SVC_ID/purge/product-994" \
     -H "Fastly-Key: $API_TOKEN"
```
4. The CDN immediately invalidates that single product across all 150+ global PoPs in **< 150ms** without touching unrelated items.

caseStudy.problem: Serving 20 billion page views per month to global readers required near-100% cache hit ratios while allowing Wikipedia editors to see edits live within seconds.
caseStudy.solution: Deployed Fastly edge caching utilizing Varnish Configuration Language (VCL), BGP Anycast, and instant Surrogate-Key purges triggered by MediaWiki database write events.
caseStudy.impact: Maintained a 98.7% cache hit ratio, handled global traffic spikes with zero origin capacity expansion, and reduced global p95 page render latency to under 50ms.

relationships.description: CDNs terminate client TCP/TLS connections physically close to users via Anycast to eliminate round-trip latency.
A CDN is essentially a globally distributed edge reverse proxy fleet with caching and DDoS mitigation.
Complements in-memory database caching (Redis) by filtering traffic before it reaches origin servers.

questions.title: Stale-While-Revalidate Directive
questions.prompt: What is the primary operational benefit of the 'stale-while-revalidate' Cache-Control directive?

options.text: It allows the CDN edge to return an expired cached response immediately to the user while fetching the updated version asynchronously in the background, shielding users from origin latency spikes.
options.explanation: Correct! stale-while-revalidate decouples user response time from cache miss latency, ensuring users always get sub-15ms edge hits while keeping data fresh.

options.text: It permanently disables origin server database queries.
options.explanation: Origin servers are still queried asynchronously in the background.

options.text: It forces the client's browser to store the asset on disk instead of memory.
options.explanation: Cache-Control governs expiration policy, not browser memory allocation.
Anycast is an IP routing mechanism independent of HTTP headers.

rubric.excellent: Explains how stale-while-revalidate eliminates origin latency blocking for end users.
rubric.gap: Confuses HTTP directives with storage hardware or routing.

questions.sampleSolution: It returns cached content immediately while asynchronously revalidating in the background, eliminating origin latency on cache misses.
questions.explanation: Use stale-while-revalidate to smooth traffic spikes and protect user experience.
